title: Architecture standards: API, coding, infra, model-serving, observability, performance & ADRs
author: Sofia Patel
content:
Overview

This page consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also documents active Decision Records (ADRs) that codify trade-offs and long-lived choices. The goal is to provide a single reference for engineers and architects to make consistent, production-oriented decisions and speed safe onboarding.

Scope
- API standards (public and internal)
- Coding standards and repo layout
- Cloud infra and capacity practices
- Model-serving standards (runtime, variants, quantization, routing)
- Observability and alerting practices
- Performance objectives and benchmarking rules
- ADRs and how to author them

1) API standards
Purpose: APIs are the contract between Redwood and customers (hosted API) and between internal services. We prioritize stability, discoverability, and telemetry.

Core rules:
- Use OpenAPI v3 for all HTTP APIs (yaml spec committed to repo under /api/specs).
- Route naming: /v{major}/{resource}/{identifier} (e.g., /v1/models/{model_id}/infer). Major version bumps only for breaking changes.
- Error model: return structured JSON {"error":{"code":string,"message":string,"details":object}} and use HTTP status codes (400,401,403,404,409,429,500).
- Idempotency: all mutating endpoints must accept an Idempotency-Key header.
- Rate limits and quotas: return X-RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After when applicable. Expose rate-limit tiers in API docs.
- Backwards compatibility: additive, preferred over breaking changes. Deprecation window = 90 days for public API unless security fix.
- Security: all public endpoints require mTLS or OAuth2; internal service-to-service calls use short-lived tokens and mTLS.

Example OpenAPI snippet:
```yaml
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerateRequest'
```

Ownership: API product managers and API platform team jointly own versioning and docs.

2) Coding standards
Principles: readability, small surface area, testability, performance-critical code reviewed for micro-optimizations.

Standards:
- Languages by service: Go for control-plane/edge services, Python for SDKs and eval tooling, C++/CUDA and Rust for latency-critical runtime components.
- Linting: enable golangci-lint (Go), black/ruff/isort (Python), clippy (Rust) with CI gates.
- Formatting: enforce via pre-commit hooks and CI.
- Tests: unit tests with >=70% coverage for non-runtime code; integration tests mandatory for API contracts. Performance-sensitive runtime modules require microbenchmarks committed to benchmarking suite.
- Repository layout: mono-repo for control plane services (/services), separate repos for runtime kernels (/runtime-kernels) with a clear BUILD/CI.
- Code reviews: at least two reviewers for changes touching API, infra, or runtime subsystems.

3) Infrastructure standards
Goals: predictable capacity, secure defaults, and infrastructure-as-code (IaC).

Rules:
- All production infra must be defined with Terraform; state stored in remote backend with enforced locking.
- Environments: dev, staging, prod. CI deploys to staging automatically; prod requires manual approval and changelog.
- Networking: private subnets for compute, limited public ingress via API gateways. All egress whitelisted for compliance-sensitive workloads.
- Secrets: use KMS-backed secret stores (managed KMS or HSM for Private deployments). Rotate keys annually or on suspected compromise.
- Capacity planning: GPU fleet capacity target = 99th percentile latency SLO + 30% buffer for bursty traffic; documented in eng-sre/capacity-planning.

4) Model-serving standards
Objective: reproducible, cost-aware, and robust serving for LLMs across Hosted/Dedicated/Private modes.

Standards:
- Model artifacts: every model has a manifest JSON with schema version, architecture, tokenizer, quantization profile, and checksum. Store manifests alongside artifacts in model registry.
- Variants: support base, quantized (8-bit/4-bit), and distilled variants. Routing policies defined in model manifest and runtime config.
- KV/Prefix caching: enable by default for chat sessions; circuit-breaker if cache hit ratio < 5% or memory pressure > 70%.
- Rollouts: canary (5–10%), gradual increase with monitoring windows (30 min), auto-rollback on error budget blowout or QoE regression.
- Quality checks: automated evaluation against golden prompt-sets before deployment; threshold for pass defined per model (e.g., perplexity delta or eval score delta).

Model manifest example:
```json
{
  "model_id": "redwood-7b-v2",
  "architecture": "transformer",
  "quantization": "q4_0",
  "tokenizer": "bytebpe",
  "checksum": "sha256:..."
}
```

5) Observability standards
Principles: telemetry-first design, fast root-cause diagnosis, and cost-conscious retention.

Metrics and traces:
- Metrics: instrument critical paths with high-cardinality tags avoided by default; use service, model_id, route as primary dimensions. SLO-aligned metrics include request_latency_ms (p50/p90/p99), token_rate, error_rate.
- Tracing: distributed tracing with 100% sampling for errors and 1% baseline for successful requests; use W3C Trace-Context.
- Logs: structured JSON logs (timestamp, level, service, request_id, model_id, message). Avoid embedding PII.
- Alerting: combine metric thresholds and anomaly detection. Alert only on actionable signals with runbooks linked.

Retention and costs:
- High-resolution metrics (1s) retained for 7 days; downsampled 1m for 90 days. Traces retained 30 days. Audit logs stored 365 days for compliance customers.

6) Performance standards and benchmarking
SLOs and targets:
- Public hosted API SLOs: availability 99.9% monthly, 95th percentile request latency <= 300ms for small-generation (<=64 tokens) common models.
- Dedicated customers: configurable SLOs with contractual targets; default recommended p95 <= 200ms on provisioned capacity.

Benchmarking rules:
- Use canonical benchmarking harness (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite). Benchmarks must: specify model, sequence length distribution, batch sizes, hardware type, and kernel config. Publish reproducible artifacts.
- Reported metrics: token/sec, p50/p90/p99 latency, memory usage, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens estimate.

Optimization guidance:
- Prefer batching for throughput-oriented endpoints with recommended max batch sizes per model profile.
- Use hardware-aware kernels; keep a curated mapping of model-architecture -> optimal kernel in kernel-and-scheduling directory.

7) ADRs (Decision Records)
Process:
1. Create ADR when a decision is non-trivial and expected to persist for >6 months (use ADR template in this repo).
2. Draft with context, alternatives, decision, consequences, and owners.
3. Assign reviewers from architecture and affected teams.
4. Publish to confluence under /architecture-and-standards and link to code/service.

Active ADRs (examples):
- ADR-2026-01: Runtime language choice — decision: Rust + C++ hybrid for kernel vs control plane in Go.
- ADR-2026-03: Quantization default — decision: default to q4_0 for cost/quality trade-off with per-workload opt-out.

Template (short):
- Title, Status, Date
- Context
- Decision
- Alternatives considered
- Consequences and Migration Plan
- Owners and Reviewers

8) Rollout checklist (for infra, API, or model changes)
- Pre-flight: automated test pass (unit/integration/perf), security scan clean, ADR or design doc linked.
- Canary: deploy to 5% traffic, monitor health for 30 minutes (latency, errors, QoE).
- Gradual: increase traffic in doubling steps (5→10→20→50) with 30–60 minute windows.
- Finalize: update docs, manifest versions, and postmortem within one week for any incident.

Ownership and governance
- Architecture guild provides quarterly reviews of standards. Significant changes require an ADR and review board approval (architecture guild + product + security).
- Day-to-day ownership: engineering teams own implementation; eng-platform owns cross-cutting CI, linting and API spec validators; eng-sre owns SLO definitions and alerting templates.

Appendix: Common thresholds and defaults
| Area | Default threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---|
| API deprecation window | 90 days | API Platform |
| Production code test coverage | 70% | Engineering teams |
| Cache eviction memory threshold | 70% | Eng-serving-runtime |
| Canary traffic | 5% | Eng-platform |
| Hosted API availability SLO | 99.9% | Eng-sre |

If you find gaps or need exceptions for customer-sensitive use-cases, create an ADR and tag it with 'confidential' when necessary.
